title: Google ships Gemini 4 Neon with 1M context and the top Coding Agent Index score
subtitle: The middle model in the Gemini 4 family lands 32% cheaper than Carbon, inherits the Carbon architecture, and takes the #1 Artificial Analysis Coding Agent score at 58.6.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon on November 18, 2026 — its fourth major model release in seven weeks. Neon sits between the flagship Carbon and the lightweight Hydrogen, inherits the Carbon architecture, and is tuned for speed and cost. The 1M-token context window carries over. Pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens — roughly 32% cheaper than Carbon. Access is via the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, the Gemini app, and Google Antigravity for paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

The benchmark story is Neon's coding lead. Google reports a 58.6 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, which puts Neon at #1 overall, along with 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high-reasoning setting. On scientific reasoning, Neon tops Terminal-Bench Science at 70.5%, RiemannBench at 84.0%, and HLE-Diamond at 71.3%. The safety numbers are the quieter headline — 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and only 2.45% shortcut rate on the coding cheating evaluation, the lowest of any Gemini 4 variant. Third-party comparisons say Anthropic's Opus 5.5 is roughly one point ahead on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and FrontierCode 2.0, so the coding lead is not uniform across every scorecard.

This release is Google's answer to the pricing pressure that OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol and Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 have been applying to the mid-tier. The durable move is positioning Neon as the production agent model: Carbon for the hardest tasks, Hydrogen for latency-sensitive loops, Neon for everything in the middle where coding and tool-use dominate. The 1M context across the family also means developers no longer have to think about context budget when picking between tiers, which simplifies agent architectures that fan out across models.

For learners: when a frontier lab ships a middle-tier model that is cheaper and faster than the flagship but wins the coding benchmark, the right question is which tier your workload actually needs. Most production AI work is bounded by latency and cost per task, not raw capability — if Neon clears the bar at a third the cost, running Carbon for everything is a waste of money and wall-clock. Price-performance on the mid-tier, not peak capability, is where most of the real economics live.
